content: Pediatric cervical spine injuries (CSIs) resulting from blunt trauma are uncommon but can lead to severe outcomes. Clinical decision rules (CDRs) have been developed to assist clinicians in identifying significant CSIs while minimizing unnecessary imaging and associated risks. While several validated CDRs exist for adults, their accuracy in pediatric populations remains unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy of various CDRs or clinical criteria for detecting CSIs in children after blunt trauma. The review included studies that assessed the performance of CDRs against reference standards such as X-rays, CT scans, MRI, or clinical follow-up. The updated search covered multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, from January 2015 to December 2022. Studies were included if they used cross-sectional, cohort, or randomized controlled trial designs to compare the diagnostic accuracy of CDRs. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for each CDR, and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. Five studies involving 21,379 participants were included, with the prevalence of CSI ranging from 0.5% to 1.85%. Seven CDRs were evaluated, with three studies directly comparing different CDRs. 1. One study with 973 participants compared the NEXUS, Canadian C-Spine Rule, and PECARN retrospective criteria. All three demonstrated a sensitivity of 1.00 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.00), but their specificities were 0.56 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.59), 0.52 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.55), and 0.32 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.35), respectively. The evidence was of moderate certainty. 2. Another study with 4,091 participants compared the PECARN retrospective criteria to the Leonard de novo model. Sensitivities were 0.91 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.96) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.97), respectively, while specificities were 0.46 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.47) and 0.50 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.52). The evidence was of moderate and low certainty, respectively. 3. A study with 270 participants compared two NICE guidelines (CG56 and CG176). Both guidelines had a sensitivity of 1.00 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.00), but their specificities were 0.46 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.52) and 0.07 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.11), respectively. The evidence was of very low certainty. Two additional studies provided indirect comparisons: 4. One study with 3,065 participants evaluated the NEXUS criteria, reporting a sensitivity of 1.00 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.00) and a specificity of 0.20 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.21). The evidence was of low certainty. 5. A retrospective study with 12,537 participants assessed the PEDSPINE criteria, finding a sensitivity of 0.93 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.99) and a specificity of 0.70 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.72). The evidence was of very low certainty. Pooling of data was not performed due to the limited number of studies and their clinical heterogeneity. Two studies were identified as having a high risk of bias. Additionally, two studies are awaiting classification, and two ongoing studies were identified. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the diagnostic accuracy of CDRs for detecting CSIs in children, particularly in those under eight years of age. While most studies reported high sensitivity, this often came at the cost of low specificity. The findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the small number of CSIs and wide confidence intervals. Further well-designed, large-scale studies are needed to evaluate the accuracy of CDRs for pediatric cervical spine clearance, ideally through direct comparisons.
